What I do know is that governing requires building consensus, counting votes, and keeping representatives from diverse districts working together to get things done. Jeffries seems to understand that responsibility, values coalition-building, and takes accountability seriously. He deserves an opportunity to prove himself. Unlike Mike Johnson, I believe he will respect Congress’s independence from the president and its constitutional responsibilities.

If he fails, his colleagues can replace him as Speaker, and voters can hold their representatives accountable. I’m confident he’ll do a better job, but ultimately, the House chooses its Speaker, and the people choose who represents them.

I don't think William Baude, a member of the Federalist Society and former clerk for Justice Roberts, is a disinterested observer. I'd like to ask him if he believes in the unitary executive theory, the major questions doctrine, and other extreme positions currently favored by the Roberts court. I suspect he does.

No one said that the court never acts independently. Yes, it reaffirmed the independence of the Federal Reserve, at the same time it gave complete control of other independent federal agencies to the president. It was half right. Its most egregious rulings were Trump v United States (giving the president immunity for official acts), Louisiana v Callais (which gutted the remainder of the Voting Rights Act), Citizens United, Rucho v Common Cause (making partisan gerrymandering constitutional), Dobbs and Heller.

I think Democrats were late to the game of understanding that the Supreme Court is a powerful partisan tool. I came to this understanding when I watched Mitch McConnell and the GOP Senate engage in numerous shenanigans to prevent Obama from appointing a justice in 2020, and to give Trump an extra justice in the final three weeks of 2024. If the court weren't partisan, why would the GOP go to these lengths? It doesn't follow.

 I think that we should reform the court so that it will be LESS political. If we can be assured of a regular turnover of justices, maybe the confirmation of justices will become less about politics and more about qualifications.

It suggests that ambition is an essential step in spurring, the development of not just proficiency, but also maturity. 

It also suggests that maturity involves venturing beyond the horizons of one’s personal ambition into a world where vulnerability (and indeed heartbreak) count for much more than proficiency and power, otherwise those who are successful as well as ambitious succumb to mere empire building.

“We also know that [tech company] founders are rewarded for extreme levels of persistence and hubris. Once committed to a mission — even a supremely risky one like building an aligned superintelligence — they will do anything but concede.”

To me, that sounds like ambition, as distinct from maturity.

Beyond high hospitalization rates and severe pneumonia, measles can trigger brain swelling that causes permanent deafness or brain damage. The virus can also leave survivors vulnerable to other serious illnesses for years. 

Preventable outbreaks also put vulnerable friends and family in harm's way, causing severe pregnancy complications and threatening immunocompromised people and babies too young for vaccines. For those of you not attuned to how to interpret research findings: .01 standard deviation difference is so teeny tiny. The reason it was "significant" was they had 3.3 million participants - so everything tested statistically is "significant". The evidence from this report is exactly the opposite. There is no actionable evidence that these bans are making any difference worth further effort. 
Teachers have been controlling phone use for decades and only wish to be able to do it judiciously, with support from admin AND PARENTS (perhaps the biggest challnege). Let them dictate use as they see fit. Why? Because they are the experts on the ground. How else might anything close to digital literacy ever occur?
 
What is the goal? Is it better test scores? The authors admit (on the report website) that sure, we could invest in the kinds of things that have 38 times more impact on student outcomes, but then we would have to invest in the things we have known that work for a long long time - smaller classrooms, student supports, classroom resources. But no, let's go after the thing that costs little to nothing but also has such a neglible impact that it will have no real effect at all. 
Invest in education for real. It is absolute folly to champion a .01 standard deviation effect of any intervention.

I miss the ability to use strictly boolean searches. Results were far better.

My father, Tom Prendergast, was UN Chief of the News and Media Division and Director of the U.N. Cultural Society and he worked directly with Carl Sagan, Ann Druyen and Jon Lomberg on selecting hundreds of photographs that are embedded digitally on these discs. Gold,as a noble metal, does not corrode. They didn't choose gold to be fancy, but for its longevity as the hope is that perhaps in a million years an advanced civilization will intercept these and decipher the messages. The info is all coded mathematics with a belief that an advanced civilization out there will employ the universal language of math to understand the contents. 
The photographs that ultimately made their way onto these discs show humanity at play, at war, using agriculture or invading other countries. There are images of people from all walks of life and of our world's mountains and rivers and pollution. He was quietly proud of this achievement while I was in complete awe. So today humanity has reached another moment of grand accomplishment as these tiny envoys glide silently through the cosmos carrying a tiny bit of us, including my dad's efforts, into interstellar space and on into a sot of infinity. Dad died on February 12, 2024. But I draw great comfort in knowing that he had a hand in this through his devotion to his work, his love of the United Nations Charter and its foundational principles of human rights and its responsibility to prevent another great war through the dignity of human diplomacy.

My late mother suffered some dementia that worsened somewhat as the pandemic progressed. 
But, to the best of my knowledge she could still live independently….until my youngest sibling decided otherwise.

When I, as the oldest, was told mom was placed into memory care I asked who was appointed guardian to decide this move. 
Wrong question. Ok. Was there a determination by a mental health professional that led to the decision. Now it is bad to worse. 
And now I am a pariah.  
I had not seen my mother for several months (I was prohibited-I believe my toxic sister engineered that) it appeared she had a stroke. 
But I no longer asked. 

She died a week later. 

Bottom line is if there are siblings make sure there is agreement that mom or dad needs memory care or assisted living. Patience is needed. 
My mother was tricked into memory care. 
I’m content I had nothing to do with it.

Maybe that's how he wants it, and at this point in his life, he is entitled to that.  Now and then, check in with him and ask how he feels he is doing and ask if there is anything you can do.  Don't use Thanksgiving as an opportunity to gang up on the poor guy.

LW1 should hire a geriatric care manager to consult with the sibling group. Hire someone who hopefully is either well acquainted with resources in the FIL area or wherever the family expects to eventually move him to. An experienced professional will have ways of potentially approaching the FIL, and/or helping the kids see the path ahead and how to prepare for it.  

One showdown will NOT produce the desired result. It took my siblings and I over two years to get our widowed stepmother suffering dementia across the country and resettled in a residential community. We started with a (unfortunately limited) Power of Attorney, but it helped once we had a doctor’s letter.  We have never had to do anything against her will, and have allowed her to FEEL independent even though we are managing every single thing. 

There is a lot involved, and most families are 24-36 months behind where the aging parent really needs to be. Good luck to them, and get some help/insight.

comments.name: Larrylaw5
comments.body: I am a lawyer with 46 years of practicing law. I work part-time for a 300 lawyer firm that has a number of newer associates who did have some exposure to AI, but learned the law the tried and true way. Last summer I used the firm's generative AI (which is converting to agentic AI as we speak) to summarize a set of facts and documents and then write an opinion letter. it took Westlaw CoCounsel about 20 minutes with something that in the past would take me 5 to 7 hours to review documents, research the topic, and write the letter. I was stunned. Quickly, I realized that this worked for me because with 46 years of experience and many years of researching and writing I could review and improve the opinion letter. It was 95% accurate, but it could not sense the political issues for my client, a public school district. So, I see two issues: how will a young lawyer get the experience of researching and reading case law and statutes which provides the insight needed to advise clients if agentic AI does the digesting  and, two, how do we train new lawyers to improve their judgment and sense of human interactions if they are unaware of the facts and reasoning of that case law and statutory language provided by actually reading the cases and investigating the facts? I know that a number of law schools have banned the use of AI. However, I know that AI will help us all in the legal profession and make us more efficient, but I hope that we do not lose the human touch.

No one posts their creative work on Blackboard where it can be fed into chat gpt; instead, students photocopy their poems and stories and hand them around. I’ve gone back to using a photocopied course pack as a text instead of posting links. I don’t want the temptation or pressure to use AI to be there at all as my students do work for my class. Overwhelmingly, students want that permission to be free of it, too. They want to use their own minds and support one another’s creativity. Our best days are when it’s warm out and we can sit on the grass outside, in the sun, where you can’t even really look at your phone even if you wanted to. My university has some kind of AI contract too, and the fact that they went there so easily horrifies me.

comments.name: ProfessorPug
comments.body: The rapid uptake of AI by university admins, eager to be sold down whatever river is on offer by tech companies, is the source of the problem here. Okay, sure, AI has or will have uses; every new technology does. But don't we know by now that we need to think carefully about how we adopt these technologies? At this point, many of us are inhabiting a world where students  pay a lot of money to learn not to read, write, or think. So they won't even know when the AI hallucinates or makes some error; they won't know how to think for themselves or read closely and carefully. If we can't see the problems with this, for individuals, for a society, for democracy, then we deserve whatever we get. Given the dying of democracy and the rise of technofascism, I think we have a sufficient foretaste to hesitate.

comments.name: Ava
comments.body:
As a student myself, I am so grateful to see the growing solidarity across our nation's campuses. Environmental and ethical concerns cannot be understated, but I find the institutional push for AI has spun out of control very quickly. Frankly, it's suffocating. I think this push has been the most felt by those of us in the Liberal Arts, whose programs are being quietly chipped away. It is hard not to see the boom of AI in higher education as part of a larger attack on academia. 

I am an undergrad philosophy student at Wichita State University, where they've recently announced our degree will be discontinued. We are one of many departments being dissolved in favor of technical training. While career readiness is important, it mustn't be to the detriment of education itself. Attending an unremarkable state school, there is an implicit (and rather classist) assumption that the Humanities are a luxury not afforded to such students– that if you want a good education, you go to an Ivy League. I worry that in shifting the burden of responsibility, we have lost the very spirit of what it means to be a public research university. 

It has been touching to see the widespread pushback against these institutional betrayals not only at my campus, but across the nation. To any disheartened readers– sign those petitions, write to your school boards or your state legislature, submit an op-ed to your local paper. Don't go quietly!

Authoritarian regimes are rarely voted in on their ideology. They arrive when people are angry about something else and the system won't answer it.
Iran is the clearest case. Most Iranians never wanted a theocracy. The old regime was so corrupt that it left a vacuum, and the best-organized faction, the Islamists, filled it.
Closer to home, Republicans lost the midterms, and deservedly so, but not over anything authoritarian. Voters were angry about fuel prices and the apparent manipulation around oil. People punish failure on everyday issues, not ideology.
The same logic explains why many parents feel they've lost a say in their kids' education. When ordinary people feel unheard, they stop caring who is offering to give them control back.
I don't think Americans will knowingly vote for an authoritarian regime, and a violent overthrow looks very unlikely. But the safeguard isn't that "it can't happen here." It's whether both parties answer people's real grievances before someone worse does.

The fragility we are seeing in our IT systems is being caused by three things:

1. AI is pushing volumes of data the systems weren't meant to handle, in ways that weren't anticipated.
2. The AI found vulnerabilites are causing us to have to make (on the fly) changes to how systems and applications are built, managed, patched, and that is breaking the paradigm that has evolved over the last 25 years.  
3. There has been a slow decline in the number of IT staff that understand the underlying infrastructure that was built the last 25-30 years.  

It is going to take a big investment in people, process, and tooling to re-engineer how we manage systems, and applications.  

We are operating under the old model and trying to deal with new threats. That is going to keep breaking and breaking with more regularity.

. Far too many data breach and ransomware attacks for far too long.  The hospital industry and government should've stepped up to secure their software long ago.  And years ago hospitals managed just fine using older plain mainframe software without internet connection.

. The Java software was developed by Sun Microsystems years ago.  But now we learn that Oracle bought it out.  We must ask why Oracle, a very large outfit in its own right, was allowed to buy up another large outfit?  Isn't that a violation of anti-trust?  Should Oracle be investigated for anti-trust violations?  It has 21 products just in hospital service.

. We're reminded that refrigeration units of stored blood in France was hacked.

We see that modern mission critical systems--life and death for patients--have grown too complex and unwieldy and are out of control.  For instance, as a patient, I asked for a Tylenol.  It took the nurse a full 15 minutes of typing to give me a pill, despite having a wristband and bottle scanner to record the transaction. Always big news when a new comic book issue lo came out in my bronx neighborhood. When I couldnt afford the dime the thing cost I would read them in the candy store by the wire rack until the owner tossed me out. I was more a DC comics elementary school kid way back when, but I used to sneak peeks at those romance comics too for a clue - any clue!please!- on how to talk to girls. 

I also loved Classics Illustrated which introduced me to books I would read much later (and found dating tips there too…I can still picture that frame in which Tom Sawyer kissed Becky Thatcher in that cave. For a 10 yo, quite the move). And I read those WW2 comics too, which gave me the briefest glimpse of what my dad, also a Jewish kid from a struggling family who volunteered to go over and kill nazis, may have experienced. 

And like so so many others, MY mom also decided to dump all those cumbersome comics and boxes of baseball cards in my room that could have provided generational wealth for our family. Sigh. It is why I guess Ive become sort of a semi-hoarder of stuff these days. Of course, it wont happen that way. It’s why that Action Comic or that Mantle rookie card is so valuable: it wasnt kept as an investment, more as a fluke. 

Again - also another reminder of the wonderful  impact of Jews on our culture. If you are an anti-semite, maybe you shouldnt act in or profit from or even watch any of the many versions of the characters he and other Jewish kids imagined into being way back when.

comments.name: Jack Frost
comments.body:
Jack was a very good friend of my mother the late Sylvia Siegel from Brooklyn.  She and Jack's future wife Roselyn were friends from kindergarten throughout their school years and into the war and beyond.  Mom was maid of honor at their wedding. She told of going to the beach with Jack, Roz and friends and then Jack would pick them up and carry them into the waves.  I have pictures of them on the beach.  Many times my mom and dad would travel to meet them at their home in Long Island and I'd enjoy the glider in their backyard.  They'd grill hot dogs for all of us kids and we'd have a nice time.  

I remember much more including when Neil their son was showing me his dad's basement studio and we threw a football into a wall and put a hole in it...Jack wasn't too pleased.  I also remember their daughters including Susan who was a year or two older than me.  Susan told how she sometimes modeled for her dad. And I learned that Roz often did inking for some of Jack's drawings.  

I'm almost 80 now but I still have the pictures my dad took and also that Jack, Roz and my mom took in Brooklyn.  Mom stayed in touch with the Kirby's until they passed away. Roz and mom would often call each other and catch up on where all the kids were and what was new.  Both had 4 children.  When the Kirbys moved to California they still kept in contact with my mom and dad.

The World War II generation was literally the Greatest Generation and we baby boomers were fortunate to be their children.

comments.name: Miss Mew

articles.title: Irish Man Sabotaged U.S. Military Plane With Ax and Chemicals, Prosecutors Say
articles.summary: Daithi O’Corrain sealed himself inside a National Guard C-130 at Ireland’s Shannon Airport in April for hours, causing so much damage that the aircraft was retired from service, prosecutors said.

comments.name: S Rock
comments.body: Funny how you mentioned guns; as expected negatively, even though there are more guns out there than ever before and the murder rate continues to drop. Perhaps if the amount of guns continues to grow the murder rates will fall further. Same logic different conclusion.

comments.name: George
comments.body: It’s likely the federal government has a hand in this success. Drug seizures, firearms seizures, thousands of fugitive captures and arrests and a focus on criminal gangs certainly could be having an impact. As a New Yorker my entire life I guarantee Mamdani will do all he can to reverse these trends and I’m quite concerned he will succeed. He’s no law and order guy. Don’t let him fool you.

comments.name: bittersweetdb
comments.body: There may well be less crime by regular citizens or gang members in US cities as compared to European cities, but how do we compare in the kidnapping/killing by agents of the state category?

comments.name: AS
comments.body:
I have tried to argue with people many times over the years that we are all safer in the US than we have been led to believe. There are a large number of people (especially conservative-leaning people, I have found) who are convinced that somehow there is more crime than ever before. Even before the sharp drop in crime in the last couple of years, it's obvious from the statistics that this country is much safer than it was in the '70s and '80s--for the most part, and of course there are some exceptions.

I won't pretend that I have all of the answers to why the crime rate has dropped, but I hope these statistics become widespread so that people can keep from being fearmongered.

comments.name: SAM
comments.body: This is patently untrue so long as you myopically look at public safety through the single lens of murder. Many other crimes remain elevated, and regular pharmacies don’t even stop shoplifting anymore because of the threat to security or other employees lives.

comments.name: Rick Box
comments.body: The rise of cell phones, everywhere, fits fairly well with a 30 year trend of falling crime rates.

comments.name: Tom
comments.body:
"And the results are pretty eye-opening..."

Respectfully, perhaps you could share them with relevance to the discussion instead of bragging points then, Mr. W-W, by telling us which societies comparatively have or haven't had similar *declines* to America's of late, instead of just presenting them as atomized single-point benchmarks to hit?

Also, just personally, I'd be more inclined to blame leaded gasoline for a violent society than leaded housepaint.  I'm sure there may have been some incidental offgassing from the latter, but the former pumped an estimated 16,000,000,000 pounds of gaseous lead directly into the breathed US atmosphere over the half-century it was in use, around 50 pounds' worth for every man, woman, and child alive during that span.

comments.name: RLL
comments.body: Great article, and gathering of statistics. Hope there are regular follow-up reports on all of this.

articles.title: American Cities May Never Have Been Safer. We Don’t Know Why.
articles.summary: Urban crime rates are near record lows.

comments.name: Jeff
comments.body: There is something very satisfying about building anything with rocks.  On our Connecticut property all you need to do is dig a bit and you'll soon have boulders and rocks of all sizes. I've been using them to build stack stone landscaping walls which manage the slope of our yard.  One project leads to another with more stone, a shed, steps to our fire pit, and a play area for grandchildren. These are all called "15 minute projects" in jest because they require considerable time and effort.  Congrats on completing projects ....eventually!

comments.name: B.A. Shipley
comments.body: Let me first say how much I admire the dream and the work - it looks beautiful. I'm not an architect or engineer, and I ask this question without malice, but what about the stone work is "structural"? It's a veneer - albeit a rather thick / deep one, but it's not actually tied into the existing structural system, is it? I'd appreciate some clarity on this. Thanks.

comments.name: Eric
comments.body: The interface between the original siding and the new stonework could be a real problem point for moisture.  I am sure they know what they are doing, but I am curious HOW they are addressing this.

comments.name: Kathy Watson
comments.body: I would really love to hear how the stone has changed the environment inside the house. I imagine it stays cooler in summer, and perhaps retains heat better in winter?

comments.name: Mark Farr
comments.body: That stone and brick-work: so deeply beautiful. Like coming across a Rembrandt in a gallery full of Thomas Kinkade's.

comments.name: BOBBY BEDFORD
comments.body: not sure this is a good idea ... an 18" old stone barrier  as a facade  on a stick-built modern dwelling... others have mentioned old stone has 1/10th insulation value modern materials, what about  ground shifts, the weight of the stone facade might cause ground compression or sink...how do you get " behind the facade " to deal with moisture-structural problems on the  interface ?

comments.name: Patricia
comments.body: Great story.   Would love to see photos of the "tree house".

comments.name: Raymond Rice
comments.body: This project reminds me of what Martijn Doolaard has been doing in the Italian alps: the patient building of stone walls by hand. I've been watching his progress for years by tuning into his eponymous YouTube channel.  Few thought he would finish the project, but he did. A stone wall is not built in a day, but eventually it comes together. I appreciated the patience and time that goes into something like this.

articles.title: Transforming a House Upstate, Stone by Stone
articles.summary: Can an architect turn his family’s new build into a dwelling that looks centuries-old? He’s getting there.

comments.name: NoSurprise
comments.body: Advanced technology is a matter of national security, and we must undoubtedly guard it. At the same time, we have to credit and respect the people making it happen.

comments.name: Eddie B.
comments.body:
"Will a Spy Scandal, Trade Friction and a Surprise Guest Ruin Xi’s Big Moment?"

I don't see why Xi would allow his "big moment" to be ruined. He has all the tools - or to use Mr. Trump's lingo "all the cards" - he needs to control the situation. He can:

1. Completly ignore the "spy scandal". And if it was raised by others, Xi can always treat it as a Taiwan-US problem, using the fact that Mr. Huang has Taiwan citizenship. He can also bring up the fact that Huang Le (Alice Huang) is a Hong Kong resident;

2. Signal he would resort to cutting off the US from key rare earth minerals once again, if the US decided to increase "trade frictions" with China; and,

3. North Korea is heavily dependent on China. Xi can let Kim Jong Un to know he doesn't want him to come to Shenzhen. That will be the end of it.

comments.name: Grunt
comments.body: There is no there there with the fact free spy allegations. Jensen Huang was not privy to any classified information, and he would be the wrong person from whom to steal chip designs—a CEO carries nothing of substance and it’s not like he can verbally divulge useful trade secrets on chip design. Even if China gets its hands on NVidia’s actual latest chip design, it can’t manufacture them—only one company in the world can:  TSMC. From all accounts, she was seemingly just a smuggler for China’s internet giants, like Alibaba and Tencent, but surely the MSS would be aware of her actions. In any event, 600,000 H200 chips are sitting in Hong Kong, barred by China from entering even though they were legally purchased. China since 2025 had ordered all of their AI companies to use Huawei chips, despite their being slower and less energy efficient. China would rather use 4x the energy to achieve AI parity through optical clustering of their Huawei chips than kowtow to US restrictions. All this nonsense about spying is just pure nonsensical politics that has destroyed $2T of US wealth in weeks.

comments.name: Juan
comments.body: I’m against almost every foreign policy decision that this administration makes, but I must say Trumps ability to connect on a personal level does make the world seem like a slightly safer place.  Xi and Putin are what they are, but culturally how you treat them in public I think matters, especially to Xi. I feel it’s the right move to be “friendly”, while playing hardball behind the scenes.

comments.name: Kurt
comments.body: I can’t help imagining how the conversation in Shenzhen will go, if the Nvidia spy subject comes up at all. Will President Xi confess: “Yes, she was ours, and a very good one. Thanks to her, we have thousands of your most advanced chips to build systems designed to defeat the very country that sold them to us”? Of course not. He will say he has never heard of her, and that China does not spy on other nations. Everybody knows that. And I fear our President will simply nod along.

comments.name: Runaway
comments.body: Greeting Trump at the airport was simply flattery. It will work.

comments.name: ksanger
comments.body: We the People should ruin Xi's big moment. When my company sent me to China to work with them to build machines for us I complained loudly. But I still went in order to preserve my pension and retire as quickly as I could. In the interim my company went bankrupt. The Chinese went on without us. While we were there they showed us a competitive machine that they had just finished copying.  There was the quiet minder sitting in on every meeting.  Her only role was to report back to Beijing on all of our technology that we were discussing. Not to mention that our Chinese businessman had a silent partner. You want to bet that the Chinese government was the silent partner?  Trump has tried and failed to stop this. He's absolutely the wrong person to do so. He's too easy to manipulate and most likely bribeable. He is absolutely correct that China is a threat to the United States. We are addicted to their inexpensive products. Our Companies are extremely embedded in China and no longer should be considered American. They have a stake and investment overseas.  Our Companies have also corrupted the Republican Party and have a huge influence in our elections.  Just think if we all just stopped, delayed, or just minimized our next Chinese purchase.  We have power.  Honest leadership could bring it out of us. The United States is unbeatable when we are united and act together. Buy Chinese products. China buys Iran and Russian Oil. We indirectly help kill Ukrainians and sponsor Iran.

comments.name: jhar
comments.body:
Xi is just being Xi -- and Trump has been working for him by helping China surreptitiously obtain proprietary American technology through his pal Huang at Nvidia. 

Xi's position hasn't changed. He holds all the cards. And Trump is the face on his Joker.

comments.name: Carol
comments.body: It might help to post these narrow, residential streets as permit parking only, give permits to residents, and allocate a parking officer to zealously ticket offenders, mostly on weekends and holidays.  Revenue raised would likely cover costs of signs and enforcement, and perhaps relieve homeowners who are entitled to enjoy their neighborhood.  The recently cleared land should be fenced off and posted ‘no trespassing’ to mitigate the nuisance and hazard.

comments.name: E Smith
comments.body: I’ve been a homeowner in Hollywoodland since 2003. There have been and always will be tourists coming to see this world icon. No one is trying to cut it off to the public. The problem is volume. It seems as if the number of tourists trying to navigate these very narrow streets has grown tenfold in the 23 years that I’ve lived here. Social media and smartphone navigation have supercharged the public’s desire to get close to the sign. The logistical and safety concerns are very real. I ought to be able to get to my house without chaos in the streets. The wanton disrespect of the neighborhood by many tourists is real. Cigarettes and trash are just being discarded in the streets. Fire hydrants are being blocked. We need beat cops and traffic control permanently stationed at the pain points to keep order and control the flow of vehicles. I love my home. I love my neighborhood, but we need a little order restored. It’s not too much to ask.

comments.name: Dave
comments.body: Parking enforcement is quick to tow. Luckily, when I parked at what seemed to be a totally okay spot, I was warned to park on the other side of the street. As we returned from our hike, a bewildered man was standing there wondering where his car had gone.

comments.name: Dan
comments.body: I have a property on a street that has become a tick tock sensation (millions of views) due to views of Downtown L A. It has taken a few years for the city of L A to do anything about it. However there is little they can do. It's terrible how unmannered the young adults are on our street. Trash, parties in the street, car races, drugs etc. So I can assure you it's much worse than the Hollywood Sign neighborhood. Note, I bought the property before this became a social media destination. It's cheap thrills for the youth.

comments.name: Linda
comments.body: Mr. Bircher mentioned the answer to the problem. Take the sign down. Having it up for a hundred years is long enough. The heyday of Hollywood has passed, anyway. Most movies aren't even made there anymore. Film production has moved out of California to other states like Georgia and New Mexico that offer more attractive tax incentives. Other countries like Canada and the UK are also used more frequently. Get rid of the sign and put it in the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures in LA.

comments.name: Chaz
comments.body: The sign is quite visible from many vantage points that don’t involve creating fire and traffic hazards and pollution. Not to mention trespass as evidenced by the photo of a woman standing on someone else’s property. Access should be severely limited here. Sure the sign has been up for 100 years or so, but Instagram has only been around for 15 or so. I feel very bad for anyone who lives up there. It is ruining their quality of life.

comments.name: Gizendorder
comments.body: Just because the sign has always been there doesn't mean that it was always a problem.  In this day and age of tourism on steroids and seemingly everyone feeling like they have to have their selfie at every site it's quite a different thing than it was even a couple of decades ago.  How many folks in less renown, rural areas have found themselves dealing with the same sort of problems because their once bucolic site suddenly caught the attention of the on line public?  it's no different than the people in certain cities in Europe who have decided that the tourism they once welcomed is now ruining their lives.  It's all just too much.

comments.name: stephan morrow
comments.body:
I spent the 90's in L.A. (brought out there by being in Mailer's 'Tough Guys Don't Dance' ) but where I ended up putting together an 'artists residency' (23 writers, actors, directors & just what you would have to call L.A. jetsam and flotsam ) on Wilton/Franklin. I would run up Beechwood Cyn to the Sunset Ranch and I remember one time there was a film or commercial being shot and the director was in awe that someone was running up that steep road. For awhile I had a girlfriend who would ride horses from there and it got to where they would just give me a horse and I would go alone into the hills and past the Sign. Sunset Ranch was a kick, 'course many things were shot there. But that road was deserted. Just a steep, dusty blacktop on a California hillside. No one but me running up it - and sometimes my girl. Can't believe what I'm seeing: a traffic jam there ?? So strange since the sign has been there for decades. So what's happened in the last 25 yrs? I lost my heart up there. Is it cursed? Had a dream of assuaging the pain by seeking some counseling from Shelly Winters RIP (I knew her well) who was nestled among the O and LL dispensing advice. The vibe going down to the flats made people do bad things as they foamed at the mouth from the disease of ambition. (everyone knew they were 3 phone calls away from being a household name). Made them nuts. (never found out what happened to her - & didn't want to). Just a bad job. 
Artistic Director
The Great American Play Series

articles.title: Fans Flock to This Famous Sign. Neighbors Say, Get Off My Road.

comments.name: Jim D
comments.body: This article made many important points, especially that electrification is a "prerequisite", that is to say, a necessary condition, for transitioning to clean energy.  However, "But even in countries that power their grids with fossil fuels, electric machines use less energy than those that burn coal, oil and gas," is too sweeping.  That is not always the case for the system consisting of the generation unit, the transmission lines, and the final use by any means.  It depends critically on how efficient the generation and transmission is.  Older coal fired plants are often so wasteful of energy, that even though the electric motors they energize are extremely efficient, the overall energy consumption is worse than direct use of a cleaner fossil fuel like natural gas in a heat engine.  Of course, it is still urgent that countries, particularly the US, make China-scale efforts to electrify, and to do so in technically sound ways.

comments.name: Gary C
comments.body: Investing in smart grid infrastructure would allow dial output up or down nuclear power sources, regional wind and solar surpluses along with battery storage to be efficiently moved around.  We’re a large modern country with many options that aren’t beholden to the petroleum or coal industries.  They have and will continue to lobby against that future.  That worked well with Trump, but we just rejected that corruption.

comments.name: MadAsHell
comments.body: I've fully electrified my home and my transportation. As a result I avoid over $9,000 annually that I would be paying for fossil fuel energy had I not electrified.  Electrifyng  is a better alternative.

comments.name: Canadian
comments.body: Can somebody please explain whay is so important to be 2, 4 or 6 years ahead of China in AI capabilities? What difference will it make for the average Joe? When the AI race will be won? Can tne US AI be ahead of China for ever?

comments.name: Critical Thinker
comments.body:
I've lived in Thailand for 8 years, during which Thailand's ties to China have increased noticeably. Thailand sells fruits, rice and other food products to China, and while the trade deficit is real, it's tolerable. This year 9 million Chinese tourists will visit Thailand. 

When I buy food products online, American products are double the price of foods from other countries. I've discovered a myriad of foods from around the world that rival the quality of US food products and at half the price. Trump's Tariffs keep American goods off of Thai shelves. 

Thai people don't care a whit about MAGA or Republicans or Democrats, but they do care about being treated unfairly by an ignorant US President whose understanding of economics is at a junior high school level. Thais are more than happy to buy Chinese goods whose quality is good and prices affordable. BYD cars are everywhere in Thailand, which has set a goal of 50% EV by 2030, a goal the US hasn't even considered under "oily" Trump.

comments.name: O'Paco.
comments.body: China has never been aggressive towards the USA. To put them in the same league as Russia,  North Korea or Iran with which she is at war is ridiculous. It is the USA that has dozens of milutary bases around China and not the reverse.

comments.name: ELCO
comments.body: US isolating itself further with these hostile policies that seek to stop China from economic development. This started with Biden, Trump wisely pulled back to seek cooperation with China, but now the neo con hawks in the GOP and Dem Party are pushing for this. SE Asia and the world sees China as the peaceful nation pursuing trade and global growth while the US continues to view others as subject to their domination. SE Asia knows China is who benefits them not the US who treats them as pawns

comments.name: Here On earth
comments.body: Sounds like the southeast Asian countries copied Jensen’s illogical theory “if we don’t sell our chips to China, China will develop their own chips”! Well let them do it. Why can’t Nvidia sell all of their chips to American and European customers as everybody wants those chips …. Musk etc. Something is really wrong. Even before all these scandals, I always feel jarring when I listened to Jensen. A person with his caliber would really believe his own nonsense? Or does he think most people are so dumb to take his words for it?

comments.name: AG
comments.body: As someone who spent four decades working in digital tech it’s stunning to me how little Americans understand that stealing ideas and innovation has always been ubiquitous. Any advantage is always short lived so the U.S. vs China clumsy honey pot spy stuff is kind of hilarious to me. I suspect the Chinese wanted to get caught in order to ping the U.S. economy. American companies spy and steal from American rivals all the time and then sue each other. I myself was once unknowingly poached by another company for what I knew. Just hung around not doing much for a year until the NDA expired.

comments.name: JRE
comments.body: Every U.S. policy is now completely predicated upon unbridled support of its business community....full stop. The well being of our country's individuals, let em eat cake.

comments.name: John
comments.body: Other than a few tech billionaires who exploit US policy variances and political system for quick bucks, ordinary Southeast Asians could care less.

articles.summary: New U.S. restrictions could jeopardize billions in investment and force countries in the region to strike an increasingly difficult balance between Washington and Beijing.

comments.name: oldwestend
comments.body: The unpredictability of Miami and its unsustainable living stress is exactly why many people are leaving big cities.  That became abundantly clear during COVID and still is.

comments.name: DM
comments.body: I guess it makes sense that DMA Design, the devs of the original GTA, were based in Scotland and in need of some Miami heat

comments.name: Slim
comments.body:
I was stranded in Miami twice over the past week due to the whims of the FAA. That city is so meh. 

Outside of Miami Beach, virtually all of the waterfront is fenced off for private access, forcing runners to congregate on “The Underline” (lol). 

An incomprehensible knot of highways have been plopped down on top of the city center with little regard for the rest of the city’s layout, so you end up with either an overpass or some cornball condo high rise looming over you at all times. 

Also, the design district is such a poorly designed let down. “Graffiti” has long been a tired, unoriginal, meaningless form of expression even when it’s authentic, unlike of the glossy, generic, mass produced looking murals plastered on every building in Wynwood (save for this weird pocket of uber expensive designer clothing stores squished up against, you guessed it, another bleak looking overpass cutting through the city).

Better to be experienced in a video game.

comments.name: Scott Colder
comments.body:
Vice City is really Overtown. I spent a lot of my time in O-Town and Liberty City scoring nickel bags of weed and drinkin' 40's ! The last Royal Castle just closed, an icon for 60+ years.
GTA6 could really use a soundtrack from Miami's finest unsung musician, Charlie Pickett. Moved away 10-years ago, still visit once a year, but the fun is gone. Replaced by  outsiders, scammers and dirtbags.
No longer the Magic City; more like Tragic City.

comments.name: JMA
comments.body: Miami. A nice place to visit, but, well…you know.

comments.name: OV
comments.body: Lived in Miami for a couple decades, then moved to Fort Lauderdale when gentrification kicked me out and traffic became unbearable. Had to leave Fort Lauderdale for the same reason. Now in CT. Can't wait to revisit my old stomping grounds via GTAVI.

comments.name: traci a
comments.body: I’ve been a Miami resident for 20+ years and don’t play video games but I love this tribute to my home town.  We are indeed all excited about GTA VI and continuing to be the Magic City in popular imagination. Thank you for a heartfelt portrait.

comments.name: Mark Dougherty
comments.body:
I’m eager for the NEXT installment: Vice City; Underwater Games.  Along with Dangling State; Help We’re All Drowning.
Go Climate Change!

articles.summary: “Vice City,” where the latest installment of the video game is set, is a stand-in for Miami in all its sunny, sexy, gritty and neon glory.

comments.name: Mark
comments.body:
China is very explicitly applying a "whole of society" strategy to strengthen itself and weaken the US in preparation for a war to push the US out of East and North Asia.

We need to stop viewing this as competition and see it as the preliminary maneuvering for WWIII.  Then we need to start acting like we are preparing for a war as well.

comments.name: Gene
comments.body: We were too generous in sharing our knowledge about artificial intelligence with the rest of the world and China learned very quickly and has almost caught up to us.

comments.name: Joseph Carmine Magnotti
comments.body: This strategy is futile in light of the number of Chinese students enrolled in our universities who are studying chemistry, biology, and other sciences, which contribute to the discovery and development of new drugs.

comments.name: mdet
comments.body: Biotech and pharma already get our tax dollars. Socialized capitalism for everybody but regular Americans.

comments.name: Chen Yu
comments.body: I run a major biotech investment firm and this article skews way too much toward the negative on the biotech relationship with China.  It ignores all of the incredible benefits. One, we start many companies in the US based on China sourced technology.   That creates thousands of jobs in the US that otherwise would not have been created.   Two, unlike in tech where we are worried about high tech leaking to a peer competitor, this is the reverse.  We are getting their novel technology.  Three, if we ban our ability to invest in Chinese companies, we can't see all the competition and that stops us from even investing in US co's because of risk.   It's important to remember we're developing drugs for patients--raising the cost or making it more difficult also increases ultimate drug pricing.  There is no advantage to creating walls here.

comments.name: an observers
comments.body: China just goes faster to test drugs and patent. In the future drug companies won’t announce anything until they have a patent.

comments.name: Osip
comments.body:
Just another example of how money and markets debases and corrupts something that serves a higher function.  

At its best science is about trust and cooperation for the benefit of everyone.  It’s a public good.  Nonrivalrous and nonexcludable.  

This article is about the problems associated with trying exclude the nonexcludable through manmade rules.  How do you profit from the public good?

But, of course someone needs to pay for science.  For years the American people have been allocating a portion of their massive collective surplus to pay for it and private investors put in their own money to bring it to market.

What this is really about is the last part.  And for a group of people who taut the efficiencies of markets and worship competition like a god you do put up quite the hissy fit when you find yourself being outcompeted.  Now you are so angry you are going to just give them the silent treatment.

I don’t understand.  If you just want to make money why didn’t you go into finance?

articles.title: An Unspoken Rule Spreads Through Biotech: Share Nothing
articles.summary: Concerns that well-funded Chinese companies will swoop in to grab new ideas for their own drug development are shaping an industry unaccustomed to such secrecy.

comments.name: Jim
comments.body:
"Motivated by the belief that improving the lives of his workers would improve his business, Mr. Johnson subsidized housing, health care and grocery stores."

Could you ever imagine Bezos, Musk, and others who have made their obscene wealth off the backs of ordinary folk ever think of doing any noble and benevolent acts such as those from Mr. Johnson?

comments.name: D
comments.body: Sometimes it's lost on folks but here it is, plain and true: Binghamton/Tri-Cities, and the whole southern tier of NY going out to Elmira/Corning were at one time among the most prosperous communities anywhere in the country.  The American middle-class was rooted in cities like these.  Endicott-Johnson, IBM, Corning Glass, and a whole massive ecosystem of other companies and institutions.  Between 1945 and 1985 the United States had created, by choice and broad policy, a wonder of the world: the most wide-spread middle-class the world had ever known.  Of course, that is all gone now.  The choices made that killed places like this constitute a crime of the highest magnitude in my book.  A crime that is on-going.  Maybe the carousels can remind us of something that was taken, a crime underway, and maybe cause us to begin the hard work of understanding that and demanding something different.

comments.name: David
comments.body: I grew up near the one in Recreation Park on Binghamton's west side, 50 years ago. I remember well the sights, sounds, and sensations. The rides were not actually free. When I started riding, in 1976, we were expected to bring one piece of litter we found in the park and deposit it in the trash can. It was a good deal.

comments.name: Dr. Cazmando
comments.body: That the wealthiest country in the world refuses to maintain its heritage is a comment to its boorish oligarchs and politicians.

comments.name: Michael J
comments.body: Where is the oldest operating carousel in the US? Watchhill, RI. Nicknamed the Fiermen's Carousel.

comments.name: Linda Brown
comments.body: What an enjoyable article that brings back happy memories of childhood. We used to go to Atlantic City for summer vacations where rides on the Steel Pier carousel were the highlight of my stay. If I got on one of the outer horses, I could snatch the brass ring to get a free ride over and over again. My mother preferred the mermaid while my dad took photos. Oddly enough, Colorado has several famous hand-carved carousels as well, as do large shopping malls.

comments.name: MDW
comments.body: I grew up in the Binghamton area and remember the carousels very well, especially the one at Highland Park in Endwell, walking distance from me. We rode it countless times, me always choosing my "fine grey pony" that was a neglected little grey horse I loved so much. I was reminded of it when as an adult and parent in New Orleans, we took the kids to ride the carousel at the Audubon Park Zoo. Kids love carousels. I hope the ones in Binghamton will ride on for generations. They are worth it.

comments.name: Michael Middaugh

comments.body: I'm not sure in what world the grandmother would be forced to testify in this case. One or the other side might ask her to, but if she wants a continued relationship with both parents it would be wise to stay out of it. I thought that she was going to reveal some bad behavior on the part of her daughter or safety concerns; it seems like she just takes issue with the fact that her daughter has a demanding job instead of focusing on childcare. There seems to be some internalized misogny going on here, and likely a disagreement between how the mother did things and how her daughter is doing things. It would be so inappropriate to try to testify on who you think the better parent is. Let them come to an agreement in court, and if you can't testify in support of your daughter don't testify at all. You would not be "doing the right thing;" you would be trying to exert your control over your daughter's work/life balance choices. A better role may be to listen to your daughter's concerns and gently try to share your own thoughts with her. The typical situation these day is for parents to share custody, sometimes even 50/50 if the circumstances allow. So even if both parents start with a request for sole custody, it is not likely that either will end up with it.
