comments.body: Reminds me of the time I lived in Seattle. On my way home from work, I would get off the bus in front of the Pike Place Market. Whatever looked good, I would buy to make dinner with. Sometimes I took a detour to grab a snack or pop in one of the shops to see if there was anything that caught my eye.  One time I snagged a pair of John Fluvog shoes on deep discount.

comments.name: Vin
comments.body: Mercado's are one of the first places to visit as a traveler. It's a first hand look at what locals are enjoying. I found visiting Madrid, no different than when I visited other European cities Mercado's . Even traveling in Brazil, where restaurants can be somewhat far and few between, Mercado's are everywhere too be enjoyed.

comments.name: Chase
comments.body:
Looking at the photos, beautiful as they are, one sees few locals apart from shoppers at the fruit stand. And the prices posted here? Definitely out of reach of many locals. 

Markets throughout Europe are a wonderful experience. It's just a shame to see so many reoriented toward the tourist trade.

comments.name: Luna
comments.body: Have a breakfast at Museo del Jamón... It's a chain and the food is good BUT the breakfast is the real deal: ham (bacon), eggs, toast and coffee all enough for two. Sit at the counter. There is one across the street up from the Prado.

comments.name: Frida's Mom
comments.body: Thank you for this delightful article. l have traveled all over the Planet thanks to my job as a science journalist. I have never visited Madrid but after reading this piece, I am inspired to move Madrid to the top of my list of cities to visit this year.

comments.name: Frutas Selectas
comments.body: With the exception of La Boqueria, the markets in Barcelona are soulless. Something about the newer markets feel cookie cutter and ordinary. The market in Sant Antoni is depressing. I avoid markets like the plague now whereas when I first moved here I actively sought out the older markets that have now been torn down and replaced with sterile generic newer versions. What's more the stalls are underwhelming: prices are higher and there's little to justify shopping in markets when you can buy better goods elsewhere. I believe in their concept but just like the former bullring, Las Arenas, was converted into a mall that could be in Des Moines, if I were the alcalde of Barcelona, Las Arenas would be the premier concert venue in Europe instead of Palau Sant Jordi which is indistinguishable from any other arena.

articles.title: For a Real Taste of Madrid, Skip the Michelin Meals. It’s All About the Markets.
articles.byline: Andrew Altschul and Emilio Parra Doiztua
articles.summary: Follow the locals to the city’s mercados, which offer culinary delights, flamenco classes and buzzy bars, all with a side of authenticity. Here are six hot spots.

comments.name: Shiloh
comments.location: Glenbard West HS Glen Ellyn, IL
comments.body: No, never. Roller coasters are meant to produce a thrill, they cause adventure seeking. Although some coasters have become unsafe, that's no reason to rule out building more. I am a huge fan of roller coasters and I don’t think we should stop building and challenging the metal to its greatest extent. That’s where all the fun is. Roller coasters aren’t just about being scared, it’s about the movement. The twists and turns, the loops, the feeling that you’re about to fly out of the seat and you should hold on for dear life. It’s about people being about to say they have finally been on a roller coaster with a loop-de-loop. Building up to the scarier rides at the amusement park is what my summer was always about. Will I finally ride it? The thrill of hearing a new coaster is coming has me jumping up and down. Pushing the limits doesn’t always result in injury. Yes there are some cases, but not all coasters cause that.

comments.name: Tyler
comments.body: In my opinion I don’t mind roller coasters all that much but some I find to be scary/extreme. Overall yes, I agree roller coasters have become extreme. I think there are roller coasters that have bad safety precautions. I agree roller coasters have become extreme because I have heard on the news that there have been many cases in which people have died/ been severely injured on a roller coaster because of how extreme they have gotten. But, it may not be just because they are so extreme and scary, it might be the safety precautions that the workers are supposed to help with the riders, that is a big factor. I still stand with the fact that they have gotten too extreme though.

comments.name: Colin Dougherty
comments.body: Roller coasters aren’t for me, but I understand why people love them. However, this is a huge issue. Safety needs to come first. As much fun as it is fun to get that thrill, it can’t come at the expense of peoples’ safety. Moreover, it’s not just simply unsafe but potentially lethal. People have been dying, and that’s way more of a problem. More guidelines need to be put in place to prevent any danger, and keep those roller coaster riders safe.

comments.name: Purnima Cha
comments.body: I usually do not enjoy roller coasters due to my acrophobia. However, when I go to amusement parks, I have often noticed that though many of my friends enjoy the roller coaster (perhaps to an unhealthy amount), it also seems very detrimental to our health. The possibility of whiplash from the rollercoaster's jerking, jolting movement also worries me tremendously. Therefore, I would say that roller coasters definately should have some sort of safety feature. I believe that one good example is in Korea, where most rollercoasters have a huge metal belt that all riders must use or else the rollercoaster will not function properly. I hope that other rollercoaster companies will also try adapting their rollercoasters to include these features in their rides to ensure both safety and amusement for the riders who just want to have fun at amusement parks.

comments.name: Amber
comments.body: I think roller coasters are exciting, but safety should always come first. Some people enjoy extreme rides, but they can also be dangerous. I believe amusement parks should focus more on safety instead of making rides faster and scarier. Having fun is important, but protecting people’s lives is more important.

comments.name: Joshua Gerecht
comments.body: I think if they make changes they need to worry about safety a bit more. I also think that the people and companies who are creating these roller coasters are worrying too much about the actual fun and should focus on that and safety. In conclusion I think some rides are too extreme which is fine if they were more safe. However a lot of them aren't if they were to make roller coasters just a bit safer I would have a different opinion though.

comments.name: ML
comments.body:
20 years ago, I went to Knotts Berry Farm on a day that was so empty, we had to wait for other patrons before they would start the ride.  None as extreme as today, nor even the Kumba I rode at Busch Gardens.  So, I was able to ride as many roller coaster that day as in all my previous experience.

At 3pm, my head was spinning badly.  I had to lie down on a bench for a full hour to recover.

Roller coasters can be dangerous.  Today, I wouldn't attempt a kiddie roller coaster because of a bad lumbar spine.

comments.name: Yelena
comments.body: Roller Coasters have always been a huge thing in my life, especially the high speed ones. Falcon's Flight in Six Flags, New Jersey, was a joy to go on. I had to beg my friend to go on with me since they weren't a big fan of roller coasters. The suspense before the big drop was terrifying and fun at the same time, as you go flying down you can feel the blood rushing up your head. My friend who’s deathly afraid of roller coasters had actually changed their mind after a few tries with Falcon's Flight. I feel like people need to get used to the adrenaline and have to trust themselves with the engineers of the roller coasters.

articles.title: Have Roller Coasters Become Too Extreme?
articles.summary: After a man died and others were injured from roller coasters this year, safety has become a concern again. Should ride manufacturers keep pushing the limits?

comments.name: Jerry
comments.body: I had to use the Halle airport about ten years ago. Security consisted of an imposing Frau giving Stasi-like pat-downs to each traveller. Security lines were horrendous. Who knows what else had not changed since DDR times. Perhaps this airport has been singled out for not being on par with Western German ones, and hence more vulnerable.

comments.name: Tom King
comments.body: So many sensible and sensitive comments from NYT readers from Europe, living as they do in the shadow of Russian interference; what a contrast to that American buffoon cozying up to his “friends” despite the electoral defeat he and his regime have incurred.

comments.name: Dan
comments.body:
Let me take the opportunity to report that no one in my social bubble here in Germany is convinced that Russia hires amateurs to carry out constantly failing attacks on the German infrastructure. We would expect that the Putin executive could be very successful at hitting us hard on a sub-war level any time if they only wanted to. We are waiting for proof, but there is nothing but hearsay in the media so far. 
What we do know, is that Ukrainian agents destroyed a submarine pipeline owned by the Germans at the beginning of the conflict. 
No one here feels threatended by either side, but we wish international diplomacy to get their act together asap and end this war. Thank you.

comments.name: Harry Haff
comments.body: Interesting that this stuff is happening in an area of Germany that was not very happy about reunification to begin with,

comments.name: Jim
comments.body: Are the Antonovs Russian or Ukrainian? They are described as Russian in the photo but Ukrainian Antonovs are mentioned in the article. Antonov is a Ukrainian company but made aircraft for the USSR so Russia likely still has many of their aircraft.

comments.name: Malcolm
comments.body: The Russian strategy of eroding the security of its neighbors with low-grade sabotage and mayhem is consistent with Putin’s behavior for the past 50 years.

comments.name: Perpetual Novice
comments.body:
What a great opening line --
"For years, Helmut Rost rode his bike to the edge of the Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany to pick dandelions for his rabbits."

comments.name: James
comments.body: While Putin is at war with most of the free world, Trump is in China bowing and scraping to him and Xi. This is just another sign that we have become another authoritarian nations endangering our way of life.

articles.title: These Villagers Wonder if They’re on the Front Line of Russia’s Shadow War
articles.summary: Russia is accused of clandestine attacks on Ukraine’s allies in Europe, most notably at Leipzig/Halle airport in eastern Germany. That has changed life for villagers nearby.

comments.name: Timothy Gill
comments.body: It would be nice if there were a map and some explanation on why they're digging in North Bergen and going east into Weehawken before it goes under the river, and showing how far it is from the current Lincoln and Holland tunnell, and what street in Manhattan it will exit at.   Also, how will the new tunnel location change NJ Transit routes?

comments.name: Riley Branch
comments.body: And those are OUR boring machines.  Musk to the rescue once again.

comments.name: Reginald V. Wedge
comments.body: Whenever the first train rolls through, Trump should be tied to the tracks.  I am not a fan of Schumer, but the Senator and fellow citizens and taxpayers deserve this win.

comments.name: Avenue Be
comments.body: And never forget Gov. Chris "time for some traffic problems in Hoboken" Christie, whose petty political ambitions delayed this project for years. Thanks Chris!

comments.name: Sharkbetty Crips
comments.body: Does the NYT need a cartographer because I’d love to apply! This is the 4th really great article Ive read today that lacked a map. In our world of decreasing geographic knowledge I believe every geographic article deserves a map.

comments.name: Stephen B
comments.body:
Hey! Those machines don't sound boring at all!

Ohhh...

comments.name: JG
comments.body: Over 120 years ago the original tunnels took 4 years to dig, passenger service began after 6 years.  One would think that our technology has advanced to the point where we'd be able to complete this faster.

comments.name: Eric
comments.body: Thank God our local governments are prevailing over the anti-infrastructure president.

articles.title: Foot by Rocky Foot, New Hudson River Rail Tunnel Begins to Take Shape
articles.summary: As the long-awaited Gateway project proceeds, two boring machines have begun digging side-by-side through some of the earth’s hardest rock.

comments.name: Stephen Holland
comments.body: Paul's work takes me back to my salad days studying at SFSU, performing in North Beach, living my dream.  So glad to have him still with us.

comments.name: DE
comments.body:
As an SF resident it’s great to get to hear about SF’s rich artistic heritage. I wish all the best to Mr. Madonna!

That said, I think there’s a secondary item here worth a deeper look: SFMTA’s resistance to proven measures that lower the danger of our roadways. For years the city has dragged its feet on road calming measures. Safer streets that accommodate our pedestrians, cyclists, drivers, and transit users should be our goal and yet there seems to be no push coming from our mayor’s office for these reforms that he ran on. 

To the SF reporters I’d say these failures are worth a story. How is city hall failing our residents who don’t have (or can’t use) cars? How much of SF’s culture has been lost due to car-based sprawl and the resulting high infrastructure costs? How do slow infrastructure projects lead to higher costs and more dangerous streets? How can SF learn from NYC in building a city hall that works for everyone?

Thanks again to the SF reporters for both this and all the other recent SF stories!

comments.name: Lisa
comments.body:
It's obviously a miracle, that he's recovered, and to such a degree that he can apparently once again create amazing works of art.

However, what this story also once again 'drives home', so to speak, is just how positively dangerous it is, simply being inside a moving vehicle.  And yet, many drivers take that very dangerous act far, far too lightly.  Heck, people seem to exercise more care, in the privacy of their own homes, using various machinery, than they do, barreling a massive 2-Ton machine through our public space, and in such proximity to others.

I really wish this country had stricter rules about not only getting a driver's license, but the ability to maintain one.  We seem to trivialize - and have accepted - a certain level of severe injuries and deaths on our roads as simply the price that the rest of us all have to pay.  Meanwhile, the occasional 'crimes' are what typically make the headlines, with crimes committed while at the wheel, put in their own separate category (i.e., not counted as crimes).

comments.name: Miss Muffet
comments.body:
"Mr. Madonna said that he has appeared in court 29 times since the crash, but no trial date has yet been set. Mr. Giron is due back in court on Friday."

No wonder the courts are overburdened. This one should be a slam dunk.

And unacceptably stressful for the person who nearly died.

comments.name: Karen
comments.body: Paul Madonna is a local and international treasure — in addition to his extensive body of artwork which is compelling and inventive,  he is an engaging and fascinating speaker and has been featured at the Lafayette Library as well as San Francisco’s library.  I’m so grateful to hear of his latest exhibit and to know he is still pursuing his art.  We are all better for it.  His quote ‘in hard times beauty can seem frivolous, but without it all you have are hard times” has stayed with me for years and I think of it now as Paul keeps creating beauty in hard times.

comments.name: rimabird
comments.body: A longtime fan of Mr. Madonna, I have saved some of the clippings, I somehow missed the horror story of the accident and so glad to hear of his recovery.  As I, myself, have mobility issues, I won't be able to attend the gallery, but will look for his book.  Best wishes to him for a continued recovery.

articles.title: His Body Was Crushed in a Car Accident. His Artistry Brought Him Back.
articles.summary: Paul Madonna, known for his drawings of San Francisco landmarks, has recovered enough to have his own art exhibition four years after nearly dying in a head-on collision.

comments.name: Robert
comments.body: Was every bit as memorable as the review although set  at some times hard to connect to story. Still the bleak expressionist feeling absolutely works

comments.name: John
comments.body: I applaud a review that focuses on what matters: the singers, conductor, and the orchestra.  Productions are always tertiary. Having seen this production in Chicago years ago with Stemme and Davidson, I disagree with the positive spin here, but that doesn't matter.  Opera is singing and music.

comments.name: Andrew
comments.body: More and more performers are singing without live accompaniment - nice the see the Metropolitan Opera evolving with the times.

comments.name: Jeffrey Irving
comments.body: While I applaud your review that is more thoughtful and in depth than most of its kind these days, I find it surprising, and irresponsible as a music critic, that you made no mention of the orchestra or the conductor leading it.  Maestro Tomáš Hanus provided the deepest passion for, and understanding of, this piece … And the Met Orchestra – as well as the brilliant cast! –  responded in kind with the sort of focused and chiseled performance that this difficult music requires.  While singers are paramount in grand opera, none of it happens without an orchestra or conductor.  And a bad version of either make any great singer’s performance a miserable one!

comments.name: Squillo
comments.body: Excellent review!  Was there an orchestra in it?

comments.name: Amy
comments.body: I wish they had chosen this opera for the HD broadcast series.

comments.name: Rebes
comments.body: Amazing performance in all respects.  But why, why, is it necessary to have two 30 minute intermissions for an opera that lasts about 2 hours.  If the Met is wondering why audiences are shrinking, this is one more reason.  Coming home close to midnight on a weekday for 2 hours of (admittedly gripping) music is a big stumbling block for many

articles.title: Review: A Fearless, Ferocious New ‘Jenufa’ at the Met Opera
articles.summary: The soprano Asmik Grigorian and the tenor Sean Panikkar anchor a production by Claus Guth that allows room for its stars’ thrilling performances.

comments.name: JJ
comments.body: It's amazing how much deliberate needless butchery people will accept, or even cheer, if perpetrated by official looking people who sell the violence as a necessary part of their job. Still true today but now the violence is on a much larger scale.

comments.name: henri cervantes
comments.body: Coca is not cocaine. Just sayin’.

comments.name: Mak
comments.body: Really,how much could a babysitter cost back then?

comments.name: CB
comments.body: Cocaine is a modern invention.  It was invented by the Germans.  The children were most likely ingesting some sort of product made from coca leaves, or the leaves themselves.  But it was not cocaine.

comments.name: LuluNYC
comments.body: Do researchers know how the children were actually killed? The whole notion is just so horrifying to our modern Western sensibilities. I find it impossible to imagine these children welcomed this role foisted upon them. Probably any reticence is why they were drugged.

comments.name: Paul
comments.body: I recently visited the museum in Argentina where these mummified children are being studied. Remarkably the children show no sign at all of fear or distress— they just look like sleeping children. As hideous as the practice is to us, the Incas saw things very differently. To appease or thank their gods, they sacrificed what was most precious to them.

comments.name: sphilipr
comments.body: I've been listening to 'The Rest is History' podcast who remark that the Romans were horrified that the Ancient Britons practised human sacrifice whilst (they wryly point out) seeing no problem at all with sending home slaves to be killed in the coliseum for public amusement. Modern American observers might look in horror at Incan child sacrifice whilst seeing similarly no problem with the ownership of guns that have twice resulted in the multiple deaths of similar aged children in American schools. In both cases it's what passes for morality.

comments.name: MT
comments.body: Anybody who has walked the Inca trail has had the experience of being offered coca leaves to help with the altitude sickness, even today. It has trace amounts of cocaine. Perhaps a more accurate picture than kids being forced to do lines of coke as suggested by the article.

articles.title: Inca Children Were Given Cocaine and Ayahuasca Before Being Sacrificed
articles.summary: A toxicological study of frozen mummies from the Andes sheds light on what happened before a sacred ritual of the Inca Empire.

comments.name: Sconseter
comments.body:
Well, with the revelation that Lutnick's (sons') firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, has many investments in those same Southeast Asia computing companies as received the Nvidia chips it would seem this should have happened a lot sooner.

But no--just another example of Trump administration grift.

comments.name: Phil
comments.body:
this under the table self-dealing orchestrated by the same person who was so disgusted with Jeffrey Epstein that he told his wife we will never meet with that man again....until the family outing to Epstein's island.

Lutnick has buttered his own bread since day one of joining Trump's cabinet and could care less of US security. He needs to be let go immediately.

articles.title: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.summary: The announcement appeared to be a response to recent criticism that the Commerce Department has moved too slowly on the alleged chip smuggling case.

comments.name: Nostromo
comments.body: Whatever you think of the original Two Columbus Circle - I personally loved it, which I know is not a popular opinion - its current façade has the verve and flair of a strip mall chain restaurant.

comments.name: Kinsalebeg
comments.body: The Donnell Library was a treasure on W. 53rd St. Such a  major shame that they tore it down and created a much smaller space beneath another luxury hotel.

comments.name: Carol
comments.body: That 2 Columbus Circle building was unattractive in its original state and is even more so after renovation.  And I had many years of viewing the building on which to base my opinion.

comments.name: acjones
comments.body:
the Museum of Arts and Design has been remade so there are windows where daylight can enter - It's a wonderful renovation inside and out - and it works much better as a museum plus a wonderful restaurant on the top floor.  Mr. Stern certainly is stern!  

the edifice of the original building meant no natural light came into the building except on the very top floors.  that's not Natural.

Mr. Stern also championed so really ugly soulless buildings as well. most deserved saving - why he is harsh about the old Huntington Hartford is pointless - it's a popular museum now and has done wonders for the artists it exhibits. lighten up Stern!

comments.name: Lomg Time Reader
comments.body: One of the places on the list is the Fresh Meadows residential complex in Queens, where I grew up. Fresh Meadows was built and planned as a complete community on the former Fresh Meadows Country Club and golf course. It is notable for its preservation of open spaces and its sense of scale. Unfortunately it appears to be under threat today as the current owners are seeking to add many new large structures in what for almost 80 years have been unique green spaces.  If this is permitted it will be a tremendous loss for those who live there and the City as a whole.  The City of Yes will destroy something irreplaceable.

comments.name: NH
comments.body: I enjoyed this article immensely. It was so interesting to see what buildings Stern included on the list and what has happened to them. Thank you for the wonderful photographs as well. This is why I subscribe to the NYT. Every day one of your journalists teaches me something I didn't know I needed to know.

comments.name: Locho
comments.body:
"we have to rise above our prejudices"

Prejudices are based on peconceived notions without factual basis. It's not prejudice to think that the lollipop building (or 2 Columbus Circle, as this article calls it) was ugly. That's just judgment, and no, we don't need to rise above our own judgments. Not every building can or should be landmarked. I'm glad the lollipop building was changed. The new version looks a lot nicer. And yeah, it's also a modernist design.

comments.name: KM
comments.body: Some of these buildings are nice, most are trash that should be purged from history. Modern architecture is a blight on the human soul.

articles.title: 30 Years Ago, Robert A.M. Stern Asked New York to Preserve These Modern Buildings
articles.summary: Two from the architect’s 1996 list of 35 have been demolished. Here’s what happened to the rest of the structures Stern sought to protect.

comments.name: LMB
comments.body: I went to Jacumba Springs last January. It was such a treat, I am going again this January--in exactly 2 months, but who's counting. Great article, thanks!

comments.name: Kimi K
comments.body: Oh my goodness, I just retired a month ago after spending the last 7 years as a traveling healthcare provider mostly in the Riverside/San Bernardino counties and driving home to SD every weekend.  I never realized there was a Dinosaur sculpture garden in Borrego Springs. This has definitely given us a few ideas for a local trip.

comments.name: Mo
comments.body: I spent a day at Murrietta.  It was glorious.

comments.name: Sue
comments.body: I spent many happy times camping at Aqua Caliente. In the old days there was an undeveloped pool up the hill where we kids played while our parents soaked in the pool. That area is full of history - it’s part of the old stagecoach route and I remember an old mission church from the 1800’s in the little town of Pala, although I hear there is a casino there. Also near Julian is Cuyamaca state park. You can hike Stonewall peak and see into Mexico. I hope it doesn’t get all developed.

comments.name: A Dewalt
comments.body: Well written, really brings you to the place.  Also, it is what makes California so incredible.   So much to do, so beautiful.  It is worth cost of admission.  Thank you.

comments.name: Kimberley M.
comments.body: Having recently retired to upstate NY after 40 years in Southern California, this was a sweet saunter down memory lane. I would add the drive up to Idyllwild from the desert area via the 74, which takes you through the beautiful Garner Valley area, or take the tram ride up from Palm Springs. Julian in San Diego County is a charming mountain community, so I'm glad to see it was part of this trip.

comments.name: S
comments.body: Great stuff. I'm familiar with the general area but love the granularity here.

comments.name: gs
comments.body: Throw in 29 Palms and Joshua Tree Park for the art and prehistoric Native American petroglyphs. And if you drive further south along the old road along the Colorado River there are rare geoglyphs too, observable from small towers and marked by state roadside signs. Only discovered in the 1920s from the air.

articles.title: Getting Into Hot Water on a Southern California Road Trip
articles.summary: Hot springs, outsider art and desert landscapes were the highlights of a four-day drive from Los Angeles to a Mexican border town and back.

comments.name: PSG
comments.body: This is an interim move. Technology companies are not headed by CFOs. Finances are much less important than technology at tech companies. The permanent CEO will be a technologist.

comments.name: Carl
comments.body:
The Board members must be aware of their own legal liability over what has happened, even if they had no knowledge of it until recently.  To protect themselves, they will not reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. 

Good.  No CEO is indispensable.  Not Steve Jobs, not Bill Gates, certainly not Jensen Huang.

comments.name: OffToMarsForGood
comments.body: A company that respects core values won't bring back Jensen Huang. Remember, employees are watching.

comments.name: Captain Nemo
comments.location: On the Nautilus, Gulf of Texas
comments.body:
I have no doubt that Ms. Kress is supremely qualified to serve as CEO.  As its CFO perhaps even more so than Jensen Huang.  

But there is more than qualifications to fill that role.  And the biggest one is charisma.  Jensen Huang has that in spades and his charisma is inseparably bound to NVIDIA.  Ms. Kress simply doesn’t have the performative skills to appropriate and exceed Huang’s that in the eyes of the investors.  The drop in share value despite outstanding enumerators clearly shows that.  With a doubling of revenue within a single quarter, the shares should have more than recovered their losses.  That they went up only a measly 2% underscores my point.

Bring Huang back ASAP!

comments.name: Not A Seer
comments.body: Employees don’t get it. Their leader broke the rules, and there will be consequences—for the company as well as him personally. He’s made their jobs harder. And who knows what other bad behavior will come out of the investigations. There is no going back.

comments.name: Balanced Noise
comments.body: The head of the Nvidia dragon has just been severed. Collette has a challenging job to steady or change the body.  60 direct reports sounds like a confucian culture. Some employees may have been touched at an "emotional level".  However, it sounds to me that fear was a bigger factor, with Jensen's daughter being the senior enforcer on the Confucian org chart.  I imagine many of the 60 direct reports were Jensen's sychophants, spies, or chronies who will be in job preservation mode, and their number one goal will to undermine Collette to ensure another of their club is installed as CEO to preserve their role and power.  From what I'm reading, I'm sure she sees it and will do what's necessary to guide Nvidia appropriately in the interim.  To do so, more than the head of the dragon will need to go!

comments.name: Jesse Lee
comments.body: The term ‘not ready for prime time’ comes to mind.

comments.name: Andrew Stevens.
comments.body: Good to see they still plan to sell to any buyer and help play both sides of the water.

articles.title: Nvidia’s Interim C.E.O. Tries to Soothe a Rattled Company: ‘We’ve Got This.’
articles.summary: At an all-hands meeting with employees, Colette Kress sought to put the indiscretions of Nvidia’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, behind them.

comments.name: SRMT
comments.body: The plot of the series has gone wildly offkey.  Not only doesn't it follow what Tolkien said about the Second Age (which left plenty of room for details to be filled in), it plainly contradicts both the letter and the spirit.  In return, there's standard Hollywood whatever...

comments.name: Gia
comments.body: The LOTR trilogy is my all-time favorite; they even inspired me to read the books, which I couldn't be bothered with as a kid when all my friends were reading them. My husband and I tried to get into the Rings of Power, but one episode into season three, and we tapped out. It was beginning to spoil the whole franchise for me, so I decided to stick with what I love and watch the movies.

comments.name: Tim Cali
comments.body:
The great triumph of Peter Jacksons production is that when people with commitment and vision (Jackson & Boykins) proposed it to a studio where the decision makers (story tellers seem to have made the decision) embraced that vision and empowered Jackson et al to expand to 3 films.  This was in a modern age a truly rare combination of vision empowered by freedom from the bean counters.
ROP by contrast is a small, myopic bean counters exploit to try to increase the dragon's hoard (what are another few gold coins worth under the mountain), and which is run by show runners that are either hobbled by the bean counters, or are unworthy of anything beyond a weekly sitcom.

comments.name: Ad absurdum per aspera
comments.body:
> “The Shadow that bred them can only mock, it cannot make: not real new things of its own.”

A thought worth keeping in mind as, Eru help us,  we enter the age of AI slop...

comments.name: Guy
comments.body: I miss poor, doomed Celebrimbor, who made the second season watchable.

comments.name: Joel Fritz
comments.body: I'm not as displeased as the author, but agree that the series could be better.  I know that the story is based on the appendix to the LOTR trilogy which I enjoyed reading 60 years ago.  It's a dry chronicle, something an academic like Tolkien knew how to write.  It could have been fleshed out better.  The major characters have some banal traits that are contrary to the epic orientation of the Tolkien stories.  I'm also not happy with the amount of hand to hand combat that includes both gross amounts of splatter and highly choreographed fencing.  The characters dance through battles lopping of limbs as they go.  I expect them to break into song.

comments.name: Macaulay
comments.body: Tolkien was an arch-reactionary who described The Lord of the Rings as "a fundamentally religious and Catholic work," loathed automobiles and the liturgical reforms of Vatican II, and was more at home in the world of Beowulf, the Eddas, and Northern mythology than in the 20th century.   That is why The Lord of the Rings is so good and so popular - no one else wrote like him.  Modernist-minded critics generally have little appreciation for Tolkien, e.g. Edmund Wilson, who wrote that "Dr. Tolkien has little skill at narrative and no instinct for literary form."   It would take a select group to do Tolkien well - his fans were fortunate with Peter Jackson.  Guess lightning doesn't strike twice!

comments.name: Al Orin
comments.body:
Was looking forward to Season One but couldn't get past the first few episodes. How could Tolkien's majestic and complex works be translated into such dull, prosaic, cliched television? The characters were flat and actually characterless, when they were not simply wrongheaded and offensive. Galadriel as petulant and pouty? Really?

The books convey elves and elvish society as enlightened and magical but the elves we meet on TV are just banal humans with pointy ears and their society is quite mundane. The same goes to a lesser extent for the Numenoreans, who live for hundreds of years under elvish guidance - and yet end up, on TV, as prosaic and uninteresting.

As the article points out, once any of these TV series leave the magisterial source material, Hollywood is unable to generate the interesting, complex, magical dialogue and stories that made the original novels so compelling. Just look at every time Peter Jackson's crew thought they were being clever and diverged from Tolkien's storyline - the results ranged from lamentable to laughable.

If I found myself ruminating at another time I paused and reminded myself of my rules.  And after my 5 minutes of ruminating I would imagine that all my problems were scattered all over my attic floor, and I would in my mind start sweeping them into a pile and them push them into a hole.  The process of sweeping minimized the problems for me and allowed me to focus on what I could control.   This is a process I have used over the past 15 years and have saved me a lot of sleepness nights.

comments.name: juan swift
comments.body: It would be helpful if the reviewer, Prof. Wood, who knows a great deal about Latin American literature, would explain that the term "magical realism" was a marketing tool and an inadequate translation of "lo real maravilloso," a term coined by Alejo Carpentier, the Cuban-French novelist, in the prologue to his historical novel "The Kingdom of this World," about Haiti. Carpentier's argument was that the surrealism that European artists sought to create through aesthetics existed in the reality of daily life and ritual in the Caribbean and Latin America. García-Márquez celebrated Carpentier's insight and expanded on it, much as the Colombian painter Botero does in his Rabelaisian vision of the Colombian ruling class. Vargas-Llosa, a realist, whose literary models were Flaubert and Hugo, uses the tools of European 19th- and 20th-century prose, as Prof. Wood observes, to critique and push back against the mythical and metaphysical in 20th-century Latin America that so-called "magical realism" celebrates. Instead of folklorizing Latin America, he writes about it with a jaundiced eye, using the tools of literary modernism. (Which is why "The Feast of the Goat" and "Conversation in the Cathedral" are two of his finest works). Although he is a brilliant stylist--better, one could argue, than García-Marquez--his lack of empathy for the poor and the marginal in his works mirrors the cruelty of the politics of his  heroes Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan.

comments.name: Guillermo
comments.body: A great novelist may not necessarily aspire to perfection in his own life, rather than that, the opposite is usually closer to the norm. Vargas Llosa had a powerful narrative that made his novels unique, with an inspiration in French nineteenth century novel, but with many other influences from Spanish and Latin American literary tradition, as well as English and American literature, etc that made his stories appealing both as an entertainment as well as reflecting a deeper connection with Western cultural traditions and creating a new form of storytelling. Moving away from Marxist revolution instead of enjoying the views from a tropical garden in Havana near Castro only showed his commitment to liberal values, while his criticism to Dominican Republic dictatorship in his novel La fiesta del chivo or criticism of Fujimori when he ran against him in Peru presidential elections also show that he was against attacks to democracy that could turn into dictatorships without any label. His consciousness about the historical decadence of Latin American countries, perhaps also about its metropoli in Spain which he also loved and enjoyed and how things could have been done differently is perhaps also one of his characteristics. He may have lacked enough social consciousness in his approach to politics but at least he wrote some of the best novels ever written in Spanish and was a staunch supporter of democracy in difficult times, which outweighs any criticism towards him

comments.name: Randall
comments.body: What a strange review, or else what a very weird biography.  I would appear from what I've just read here, that either the reviewer has failed to read the full scope of Vargas Llosa Nobel prize winning life's accomplishments.  Or are they simply , both or one or the other, insensitive to the range of the author's interests, or of the influence of French literature and the history of the DeGaulle 5th Republic years on his writing and political development in the 1970s.  It seems particularly curious that either the review or the biographer found Vargas Llosa's turn away from the revolutionary left in response to the Shining Path destruction of Peruvian social and financial stability, or the corruption of the forces that brought the Japanese immigrant and later prisoner convicted not only of theft but of connivance in assassination to the Peruvian presidency.  As an admirer of Vargas Llosa's witty social commentary on romance, the Latin lover, popular entertainment on radio and television, the perils of youthful lust and geriatric priapism, rustic elopement, the terror of riding a bus into Shining Path territory, the primitive Marxism of urban guerrillas who could never decide on an action.  And then to say he wrote 4 good books, and the 3 first were his best.  I guess I'll have to wait for a real biography or a better informed reviewer.

Based on my reading, it seems that what’s needed at the core may be both recalibrated fiscal policy and growth-oriented monetary policy.

Given the level of the national debt and the credit-heavy nature of the consumer economy, the Fed might want to consider pursuing policies that lower interest rates to curb any lingering concerns of a potential illiquidity or insolvency situation leading to currency and bond crises - however unlikely that may be - as well as to avoid triggering slower growth or a recession.

At the same time, the government should look into using targeted fiscal and regulatory solutions to raise taxes on upper-middle-class and wealthy households, perhaps by reducing various tax deductions. The government could also consider raising the federal estate tax rate while simultaneously lowering the exemption from the current $15 million.

While the debt limit is largely a symbolic and political measure that could eventually be removed, I wonder about the timing of it and how abolishing it now might be perceived by the market in terms of its perceived potential influence on inflation.

That’s my two cents.

Panguna is not only copper. There is gold and silver in the ore, and these extra metals often decide whether a mine pays. The regional government has already brought in a new partner to reopen it.
We tend to read this as a story about one company. But the demand comes from us. Much of the world’s gold goes to jewelry, investment bars and central bank vaults, not clean energy. Less than half of the copper in old products is recycled. So the green transition still runs through places like Bougainville, where the cost has landed on the community in extreme environmental damage and a brutal civil war.
$250 million for 25,000 people and a buried river system is a start. Is it possible to call a transition just if it repeats this sequence somewhere else? Perhaps society as a whole needs to take more responsibility.

comments.name: RDJ
comments.body:
Gene expression is one thing. The interaction of the gene products is quite another.

Many genes produce mRNA messages that are translated into proteins. Some of these proteins have enzymatic activity that underlies metabolism, and structural properties that underlies . . . Well, structure. Some of them have inhibitory or promoting effects on the activity of other proteins, or on the expression of other genes.

Other genes produce non-protein-coding RNAs that may have enzymatic activity themselves, or have excitatory or inhibitory effects on gene expression or protein translation.

And there are many small molecules that participate in these interactions. ATP, cAMP, cGMP, calcium and magnesium, and others. Their levels are regulated by protein activity.

All of these factors form an extremely complex network of positive and negative interactions. And all this goes on in the context of a membrane-enclosed space, within which there are other structures that serve specific purposes (mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, etc.)

Genes are the seeds; the cell is an entire rain forest.

A working model of the cell must include the details of this network. I cannot tell from this article whether these virtual cells do or not.
